common_name: Boskoop Giant Black Currant (Historic Dutch Black Currant)

planting.note: Plant dormant bare-root or container shrubs in fall or very early spring in fertile, moisture-retentive soil in full sun to partial shade; Boskoop Giant is self-fertile and does not need a second bush for pollination.

directions: Boskoop Giant is one of the oldest black currant cultivars still commercially available, originating from the Dutch nursery town of Boskoop around the turn of the twentieth century and prized for its vigorous growth and unusually large, aromatic berries borne on long strigs. Because Ribes nigrum is a highly effective alternate host for white pine blister rust, confirm this cultivar is legal to plant in your state or county before ordering, since several eastern and midwestern jurisdictions restrict or ban black currants outright. Give plants rich, evenly moist soil and full sun to light shade, and renew the bush each dormant season by removing wood older than three years, since Boskoop Giant fruits most heavily on one- and two-year-old canes. The intensely flavored fruit is better suited to jam, syrup, and cassis production than fresh eating, and the bush's older, less disease-resistant genetics mean it benefits from good air circulation to limit leaf spot and mildew.
sources: National Fruit Collection, Brogdale (Ribes nigrum 'Boskoop Giant')
Cornell University Cooperative Extension — Currant and Gooseberry Production

planting.note: Plant dormant bushes from fall to early spring in cool, well-drained soil; Greenfinch carries an RHS Award of Garden Merit for its compact, nearly upright habit and heavy, reliable cropping.

directions: Greenfinch was bred at England's East Malling Research Station specifically to combine strong resistance to American gooseberry mildew with a tidy, semi-upright bush that is far easier to pick than sprawling older varieties. Because it is a Ribes species, check local regulations before planting, as gooseberries can be restricted in areas managing white pine blister rust. The medium-sized, smooth pale green berries hold their tart flavor well and are excellent for pies, sauces, and preserves, though they also sweeten enough for fresh eating if left to fully ripen. Keep roots cool with mulch and prune out the oldest third of the wood each winter to maintain the open framework that keeps this compact cultivar productive and easy to harvest.
sources: East Malling Research — Gooseberry Breeding Archive
Ken Muir Nursery (UK) — Gooseberry Variety Guide

common_name: Langley Gage Gooseberry (Historic English Dessert Gooseberry)

planting.note: Plant dormant bushes from fall to early spring in cool, humus-rich soil with afternoon shade in warm climates; Langley Gage is a compact, lower-vigor heirloom kept in national fruit collections for its sweet, translucent dessert berries.

directions: Langley Gage is a small, historic English gooseberry maintained today mainly in heritage fruit collections, grown for its small, near-translucent pale greenish-white berries with an unusually sweet flavor that makes it one of the better gooseberries for eating fresh off the bush rather than cooking. As with other Ribes, confirm it is permitted in your state or county before planting, since gooseberries can carry white pine blister rust between white pines and their alternate hosts. The bush itself is notably compact and low-vigor compared to modern culinary gooseberries, so it suits a small border or container culture better than a production row. Give it cool, humus-rich soil, mulch to conserve moisture, and thin out crowded interior branches each dormant season to keep the small fruit clean and easy to reach among the thorny stems.
sources: National Fruit Collection, Brogdale (Ribes uva-crispa 'Langley Gage')

common_name: White Versailles Currant (Classic French White Currant)

planting.note: Plant dormant hardwood-cutting-grown bushes in fall or very early spring into fertile, moisture-retentive soil; White Versailles is a nineteenth-century French heirloom and is self-fertile.

directions: White Versailles is a long-cultivated French white currant, dating to the nineteenth century, valued for its vigorous growth and long, well-filled strigs of large, pale golden-pink berries with a mild, honeyed flavor milder than most red currants. Ribes species are restricted or banned in some states and counties as alternate hosts for white pine blister rust, so verify local rules before ordering plants. The vigorous, upright bush establishes quickly and tolerates a wider range of soils than many currant cultivars, though it still fruits best with consistent moisture and a mulched, cool root zone. Because fruit forms on older spurwood, prune out only the oldest third of stems each winter rather than cutting hard, and net ripening clusters against birds, which find the pale, glowing fruit just as attractive as red currants.
sources: National Fruit Collection, Brogdale (Ribes rubrum 'White Versailles')

common_name: Stanza Red Currant (Late-Season Norwegian Red Currant)

planting.note: Plant dormant bushes in fall or early spring in fertile, cool soil; Stanza was bred in Norway for late ripening and extends the red currant harvest well past earlier cultivars like Jonkheer van Tets.

directions: Stanza is a Norwegian-bred red currant selected for ripening several weeks later than standard cultivars, which makes it a useful choice for stretching the fresh currant harvest into late summer or for cooler northern gardens where early cultivars ripen unevenly. Like other Ribes, it can be regulated as a white pine blister rust host, so check state or county rules before adding it to the garden. The upright, hardy bush is self-fertile and holds its glossy red berries well on the strig without splitting, which makes for a cleaner harvest and less fruit loss to rain. Grow it in full sun to light shade in evenly moist, fertile soil, and prune out the oldest quarter of the wood each dormant season to keep new, productive spurwood coming.
sources: NIBIO (Norwegian Institute of Bioeconomy Research) — Currant Cultivar Trials
Cornell University Small Fruit Production Guide

planting.note: Plant container-grown or bare-root shrubs in early spring in full sun to part shade; Galicjanka is a Polish-selected cultivar bred for high, reliable fruit yields and is self-fertile.

directions: Galicjanka is a Polish-bred black chokeberry that became one of the most widely planted cultivars in Central Europe's commercial aronia industry, chosen for consistently heavy fruit set and berries with very high anthocyanin and polyphenol content, a trait studied extensively in food-science literature on aronia juice and supplements. The upright, vigorous shrub produces abundant white spring flowers followed by dense clusters of glossy black fruit that ripen in late summer, with astringent raw flavor that is better suited to juice, syrup, and jam than fresh eating. It adapts to a wide range of soils, including damp or heavy ground where many other fruiting shrubs struggle, though it performs poorly in shallow, chalky soils unless amended. Little pruning is required beyond removing the oldest canes every few years to keep the planting productive, and fall color turns a vivid red-orange before leaf drop.
sources: Research Institute of Horticulture, Skierniewice, Poland — Aronia melanocarpa Cultivar Descriptions
Journal of Applied Botany and Food Quality — Aronia melanocarpa Cultivar Studies
University of Minnesota Extension — Aronia Cultivar Selection
